sourceNotes: Seeded from PFN roleplay performance indicators and finance cluster exam data.
Drawn in three tiers: PFN event flavor first, then this event's own instructional areas woven with the rest of the finance cluster exam blueprint.
Terms are scoped for future vocab-card, quiz, and event-filter UI use.

terms.definition: The legal capacity in which deposits are held — single, joint, revocable trust, certain retirement, business — each of which carries its own separate $250,000 of coverage at the same insured bank, so one household can be fully covered well past $250,000 without opening an account anywhere else.
terms.whyItMatters: A PFN roleplay where a client with $600,000 asks whether they must move money to a second bank is answered by re-titling across categories, and the judge wants the per-category arithmetic, not a warning.

terms.definition: Coverage that reaches each underlying owner of funds an agent, fiduciary or fintech places at an insured bank, up to $250,000 apiece, but only when the account is titled to disclose the custodial relationship and someone's records identify every owner and their share.
terms.whyItMatters: Advising a payroll or prepaid-card program on why it must keep an owner ledger — and telling a customer of a failed fintech partner what they actually recover — turns on those two recordkeeping conditions.

terms.definition: The federal floor for when a deposit must be withdrawable: cash, wires, government and cashier's checks and the first $275 of a day's check deposits are available the business day after deposit, with most of the remainder due by the second business day.
terms.whyItMatters: A teller-window roleplay asking when a customer can spend a $2,000 check is scored on splitting the deposit into the next-day slice and the rest, not on answering 'a few days.'

terms.definition: A longer availability delay — up to seven business days — a bank may impose only when a deposit trips a named trigger: an account open less than 30 days, check deposits above $6,725 in one day, a redeposited or repeatedly overdrawn item, or reasonable cause to doubt collectibility, and only with written notice to the depositor.
terms.whyItMatters: When a customer disputes a hold on a large check deposited into a two-week-old account, judges expect the competitor to name the specific trigger and the notice requirement rather than citing bank policy.

terms.definition: Under UCC Article 4 a paying bank must return or dishonor an item by midnight of the banking day following the banking day it received it; miss that clock and the bank is accountable for the full amount even though the check was never good.
terms.whyItMatters: Returned-item and check-fraud roleplays hinge on it: once the deadline passes the loss sits with the paying bank, which decides whether the branch tells the customer to pursue the writer or the bank.

terms.definition: A paper reproduction of both sides of an original item that Check 21 makes the legal equivalent of the original when it bears the required legend, and whose recipient may demand expedited recredit of up to $2,500 within ten business days if it was charged in error.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where a customer claims a duplicate posting from a check image is answered with the recredit ceiling and the ten-day clock, not with a promise to research it.

terms.definition: One of three daily submission cutoffs that let an originator settle an electronic entry the same banking day instead of the next one or two, subject to a per-entry cap of $1,000,000 and a requirement that the receiving bank make the funds available by 5:00 p.m. local time.
terms.whyItMatters: Payroll-correction and emergency-vendor-payment roleplays turn on whether the competitor knows the cap and the availability time, or reaches for a wire and its fee by default.

terms.definition: How long a receiving bank has to send an entry back as unauthorized — 60 calendar days from settlement for a consumer debit, on the customer's written statement, against only two banking days for a business debit, which is why corporate accounts buy debit blocks and filters.
terms.whyItMatters: A small-business client who finds a bad debit three weeks later is already out of time, so the roleplay answer is ACH positive pay, and it only lands if the competitor knows the two-day figure.

terms.definition: The principle that a Fedwire payment settles gross and in real time and cannot be recalled once the receiving bank accepts it, so recovering a mistaken or fraud-induced transfer depends entirely on the beneficiary bank's cooperation — unlike ACH, whose return rights are measured in days.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-email-compromise roleplays are scored on advising the client that the wire is gone and the ACH is not, and on choosing the rail before the payment leaves.

terms.definition: The stepped cap on what a consumer owes for unauthorized electronic transfers: $50 if the lost card or statement is reported within two business days of learning of the loss, $500 if reported after that but within 60 days of the statement, and unlimited losses for transfers occurring past the 60-day mark.
terms.whyItMatters: A debit-card fraud roleplay is won by telling the customer which tier the timing of their call puts them in — a graduated exposure that has no counterpart on the credit-card side.

terms.definition: An instruction not to pay an item, which under UCC 4-403 lapses after 14 calendar days if given orally and never confirmed in writing, runs six months in written form and is renewable, and which cannot reach a cashier's or certified check the bank has already obligated itself on.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where a customer wants to halt a check written to a bad contractor is scored on the oral-versus-written clocks and on the certified-check exception.

terms.definition: A batch-sequencing practice that posts a day's debits largest first, draining the balance before the small items clear and multiplying the number of overdraft fees charged on exactly the same set of transactions a chronological run would have covered.
terms.whyItMatters: Bank ethics and consumer-fairness roleplays ask the competitor to work a four-transaction example and show that the ordering, not the balance, produced the fee count.

terms.definition: The affirmative, advance consent a bank must obtain on a segregated notice before it may charge overdraft fees on ATM withdrawals and one-time debit card purchases — consent that checks, ACH debits and recurring payments do not require, so those items can overdraw an account whether or not the customer ever agreed.
terms.whyItMatters: Explaining why one $35 fee must be refunded and an identical one need not be depends on sorting the transaction into the opt-in half or the exempt half.

terms.definition: The deposit-side disclosure law that forces a bank to quote a 365-day annual percentage yield rather than a nominal rate, to state the minimum balance needed to earn that yield in any advertisement of it, and to give 30 days' advance written notice before a change that reduces the customer's return.
terms.whyItMatters: A savings-account roleplay comparing a 4.9% nominal rate against a 4.95% yield is scored on which figure the law makes comparable and on the notice owed before the bank cuts it.

terms.definition: The disclosure a financial institution owes when a customer relationship begins, and annually unless it qualifies for the exception, naming the nonpublic personal information it shares and giving a reasonable opportunity — commonly 30 days — to opt out of sharing with nonaffiliated third parties, an opt-out that does not reach affiliates or joint-marketing partners.
terms.whyItMatters: A data-sharing roleplay is scored on drawing the line between sharing the customer can stop and sharing they cannot, plus the timing of the notice they should already have received.

terms.definition: The standard for U.S. equities, corporate bonds and municipal securities since May 28, 2024, under which cash and securities change hands one business day after the trade date — halving the window a buyer has to fund the account and compressing every date that keys off settlement.
terms.whyItMatters: A brokerage-service roleplay asking when sale proceeds can be wired out is answered from trade date plus one, and the shortened cycle is what makes unsettled-funds violations easier to trip.

terms.definition: The first trading day on which a buyer no longer acquires the declared distribution; under one-business-day settlement it now falls on the record date itself, so shares bought that morning pay the dividend to the seller and the price typically opens lower by roughly the dividend amount.
terms.whyItMatters: Investing roleplays that ask when a client must own a stock to collect the quarterly payout are scored on this date, not on the declaration or payable date.

terms.definition: A cash-account infraction committed by selling a security that was bought with funds not yet settled, before those funds settle; three of them inside a rolling twelve months restricts the account to settled cash only for 90 days.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay with a client trading in and out of positions in a cash account turns on that count and the 90-day restriction, which a margin account avoids entirely.

terms.definition: The Federal Reserve's cap on the credit a broker may extend on a new purchase — 50% of the price — so a $20,000 position requires at least $10,000 of the investor's own money, and a call is issued when the deposit falls short.
terms.whyItMatters: Leverage roleplays are scored on computing the buying power a $10,000 deposit creates and on separating this one-time requirement from the ongoing FINRA maintenance level.

terms.definition: A demand for cash or securities triggered when the investor's equity drops below the ongoing minimum — 25% of market value under FINRA rules and often 30% or more at the firm — which after a 50% initial purchase means roughly a one-third price decline sets it off.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay asking how far a leveraged position can fall before the client hears from the broker is answered with that percentage and the resulting price, not with a vague warning about risk.

terms.definition: Protection of up to $500,000 per customer per capacity at a failed brokerage, of which no more than $250,000 may be cash, and which restores missing securities from the firm's failure only — a portfolio that simply lost value is not covered at all.
terms.whyItMatters: A client who mistakes brokerage protection for deposit insurance is a standard PFN roleplay, and the answer is the cash sub-limit plus the exclusion of market losses.

terms.definition: A FINRA designation applied to a margin account that makes four or more same-day round trips within five business days when those trades exceed 6% of total activity, after which the account must hold at least $25,000 in equity before it may day trade again.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay with a student client who wants to trade actively is scored on naming both the four-trade count and the $25,000 floor, a threshold no cash account requirement matches.

terms.definition: What a quoted nominal rate actually returns over a year once compounding inside that year is counted, computed as (1 + i/n)^n minus 1 — so 12% compounded monthly is 12.68% and compounded daily is 12.75%, and it is the only basis on which two differently compounded offers can be compared.
terms.whyItMatters: Choosing between a 5.90% quarterly-compounded CD and a 5.85% daily-compounded one is a live PFN case, and nothing but this conversion decides which pays more.

terms.definition: A stream of equal payments made at the beginning of each period instead of the end, so every payment earns one extra period of interest and both its present and future values equal the ordinary-annuity figures multiplied by (1 + i).
terms.whyItMatters: Lease payments and insurance premiums are annuities due; using the ordinary-annuity factor understates the answer by exactly one period of interest and loses the item.

terms.definition: Depositing an item by transmitting an image from a phone or scanner instead of presenting the paper, which shifts duplicate-presentment risk onto the depositor and is why banks require a restrictive endorsement and retention of the original for a stated period.
terms.whyItMatters: A small-business onboarding roleplay asks what the customer must write on the back of the check and how long to keep it, which is the entire control for this channel.

terms.definition: A check drawn on the same bank that takes it for deposit, so it never enters interbank collection and posts on that bank's own books, which is why it can be made available faster than a transit item cleared through the Federal Reserve or a correspondent.
terms.whyItMatters: Explaining why one deposited check clears overnight and another takes two days begins with sorting the item into this category or the transit category.

terms.definition: A presented check or ACH debit the bank returns unpaid because the collected balance will not cover it, charging the payor a returned-item fee — as distinct from paying it into a negative balance, which produces an overdraft fee instead and leaves the payee holding good funds.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay about a bounced rent check is scored on which of the two fees the account actually took, and on the fact that re-presentment can generate the charge a second time.

terms.definition: Holding securities in a broker-dealer's nominee name for the customer, with beneficial ownership tracked on the firm's books and the position immobilized at a central depository — the arrangement that makes one-day settlement and instant transfer possible while routing proxies and dividends through the broker.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where a client asks for a paper certificate is answered by explaining what registration form the account already uses and why the settlement cycle depends on it.

terms.definition: The network of people and activities moving a product from raw materials to the customer.
terms.whyItMatters: Supply-chain thinking underlies inventory, vendor, and cost decisions.

terms.definition: A respondent scoring 0 to 6 on the 0-to-10 recommend question; 7 and 8 are passives and 9 and 10 are promoters. Passives are dropped from the calculation entirely rather than counted as neutral, so nudging a 6 up to a 7 raises the score while nudging a 7 up to an 8 changes nothing at all.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay deciding where a limited service-recovery budget goes is settled by which score band the customer sits in, not by how upset they sound.

terms.definition: Aristotle's rhetorical syllogism, in which one premise is deliberately left unspoken because the audience already believes it and will supply it themselves. 'We should sponsor the tournament - our customers are all high school families' hides the premise that reaching high school families is worth what the sponsorship costs. The unstated premise is where the argument is strongest with a friendly audience and weakest with a hostile one, because attacking what was never said aloud is easier than attacking what was.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items that ask what assumption a memo's recommendation rests on are asking you to recover exactly this missing premise.

terms.definition: The value of mutually beneficial trades destroyed when price is pushed away from the market-clearing level by a tax, a ceiling, a floor or a monopoly. On a supply-and-demand diagram it is the triangle between the two curves over the lost quantity — one-half base times height — and it goes to no one: not the buyer, not the seller, not the government.
terms.whyItMatters: Items ask who bears the cost of a per-unit tax and answer with the split of the burden plus this un-captured loss; naming only the tax revenue is an incomplete answer.

terms.definition: Money held by a neutral third party until an obligation is met — in a mortgage, the monthly share of property taxes and insurance the lender collects and pays out.
terms.whyItMatters: It explains why a mortgage payment exceeds principal and interest in a home-buying scenario, and why it changes when taxes are reassessed.

terms.definition: Failure to exercise reasonable care that results in injury or loss to another.
terms.whyItMatters: It is the most common tort in business and a leading source of liability claims.

terms.definition: An arbitrary system-generated identifier — normally an auto-incrementing integer — carrying no business meaning, chosen over a natural identifier such as an email address or a part number precisely because the business can change the natural value. When a supplier renumbers all 4,000 of its parts, rows keyed on the part number break every reference pointing at them; rows keyed on the integer do not move at all.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay on migrating a supplier catalog asks which column should identify a part; picking the meaningful one is what forces the rework the judge is listening for.

terms.definition: The advancement path within an organization based on skills, performance, and leadership.
terms.whyItMatters: Understanding progression guides career decisions in higher-level scenarios.

terms.definition: Book inventory value minus counted physical value, divided by book value (or by net sales), expressed as a percentage — it isolates loss to theft, damage, spoilage and paperwork error, and never includes units legitimately sold.
terms.whyItMatters: Loss-prevention items give a recorded value and a counted value and ask for the percentage lost; the retail benchmark of roughly one to two percent of sales is what a judge compares your figure against.

terms.definition: Ranking complaint categories by volume and cutting where the cumulative share crosses about 80% — if billing errors, late delivery and wrong item are 82% of 1,000 complaints, the remaining eleven categories split 18% and wait. Because it sorts on frequency alone, a rare category that costs the most per case needs a severity weight before it is set aside.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay handing over a year of complaint data expects the vital few named and the severity caveat stated out loud.

terms.definition: In speech act theory (Austin and Searle), the action a speaker performs in saying something - promising, ordering, warning, refusing - as distinct from the locutionary act, which is the literal words and their sense, and the perlocutionary act, which is the effect actually produced in the hearer. 'It is cold in here' is locutionally a remark about temperature, illocutionarily a request, and perlocutionarily successful only if somebody closes the window.
terms.whyItMatters: A service roleplay in which the customer says 'I have been waiting a while' is scored on whether you answer the request rather than the sentence.

terms.definition: Emotional self-perception measured as a personality disposition: instruments such as the TEIQue ask a person to agree or disagree with statements about themselves across roughly fifteen facets, so the score records self-belief and overlaps heavily with the Big Five. Ability EI, by contrast, is scored on correct answers to emotion problems, which is why the two kinds of measure correlate only weakly with each other.
terms.whyItMatters: A human resources roleplay in which a candidate proposes an EI screen for hiring is judged on knowing that a self-report inventory can be gamed by an applicant while a performance test cannot.

terms.definition: The principle that adding more of one input eventually yields less added output.
terms.whyItMatters: It explains why scaling operations becomes less efficient past a point.

terms.definition: A court-supervised liquidation discharging most unsecured debts by selling non-exempt assets, unlike a Chapter 13 filing, which keeps assets under a multi-year repayment plan.
terms.whyItMatters: Debt-control scenarios test that student loans and most taxes survive discharge, and that the filing sits on a credit report for a decade.

terms.definition: The enforced rule that every foreign-key value must match a primary-key value that actually exists in the parent table; with it turned on the engine rejects an orphan child row outright, and a delete of a parent must either cascade to its children or be refused, never silently leave them stranded.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay about a corrupted customer database usually ends with the judge asking what stops a deleted account from leaving unreachable orders behind, and this constraint is the answer.

terms.definition: Investment credential awarded after passing three sequential exams, each historically about six hours, and documenting 4,000 hours of qualified work experience earned over a minimum of 36 months. It certifies analytical competence only: unlike a CPA license it grants no legal authority to audit financial statements or sign a tax return.
terms.whyItMatters: In a business-finance roleplay explaining designations to an intern, the tested contrast is that this one signals analysis while the CPA license signals attest authority.

terms.definition: Coordination among suppliers, makers, and distributors to optimize flow and cut cost.
terms.whyItMatters: Collaboration reduces delays and strengthens competitive advantage.

terms.definition: The half of a job-analysis output that describes the person rather than the work — required education, licensure, years of experience, skills and physical requirements. Its companion, the job description, lists the duties, reporting relationship and working conditions of the position itself; a screening decision must be traceable to the specification, because a requirement that appears nowhere in it is very hard to defend as job related.
terms.whyItMatters: Building a posting in a hiring roleplay is scored on separating what the job does from what the person must bring, which is where invented requirements get caught.

terms.definition: A four-step frontline script — listen without interrupting, apologize for the impact rather than admitting fault, solve inside the agent's own authority, thank the customer for reporting it. It ends at the individual fix, whereas the HEARD sequence appends a diagnose step that pushes the cause back into the process, so LAST alone leaves the failure free to recur.
terms.whyItMatters: A difficult-customer roleplay is scored step by step, and the absent diagnose step is what separates a passing recovery from a winning one.

terms.definition: A sentence that does not describe an act but carries it out, so it cannot be true or false - only successful or void: 'I accept your offer,' 'I resign,' 'I hereby order 500 units.' Austin's felicity conditions are what make it stick - the right person, the right circumstances, the right form - which is why a casually typed 'agreed' from an authorized employee can create a binding acceptance while a long email full of enthusiasm creates nothing.
terms.whyItMatters: Digital-risk items that ask how a staff member bound the company in a chat message turn on this distinction between describing and doing.

terms.definition: Passes a strict two-part test: non-excludable, meaning a non-payer cannot be kept from using it, and non-rival, meaning one person's use does not reduce what is left for anyone else. National defense and a lighthouse qualify; cable television is excludable and a crowded highway is rival, so neither does — which is why private firms underprovide the real thing and taxes fund it.
terms.whyItMatters: Items list several government-provided services and ask which genuinely meets the economic definition; roads, schools and parks fail one prong each and are the intended distractors.

terms.definition: The bureau's file of a consumer's accounts, balances and payment history — the underlying record, not the three-digit number calculated from it.
terms.whyItMatters: A client disputing a score in a roleplay has to correct the report first, since the score is only a summary of what the report says.

terms.definition: Keeps every row of the first table and fills the second table's columns with NULL wherever no match exists — those same 120 order-less customers come back, so COUNT(*) returns 500 while COUNT(order_id) returns 380, and the 120-row gap between the two counts is precisely the set that had no match.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked to list customers who bought nothing this quarter, the competitor has to name this join and then filter on the NULL — the inner join cannot produce that list at all.

terms.definition: Environmental marketing claims the seller cannot substantiate, policed in the United States by the FTC's Green Guides at 16 CFR Part 260, which treat unqualified general claims such as 'eco-friendly' or 'green' as deceptive because they imply every possible environmental benefit, and require a degradability claim to mean complete breakdown within one year of customary disposal; a truthful narrow claim must therefore be stated narrowly to be lawful.
terms.whyItMatters: Sustainability roleplays that ask you to approve a packaging claim are scored on naming the standard and qualifying the claim, since an unqualified benefit statement is a legal exposure, not just a marketing choice.

terms.definition: Two-part credential in financial planning, analysis and strategic decision support, requiring a bachelor's degree, two years of management-accounting experience, and 30 continuing hours a year of which 2 must be ethics. It is built for internal decision support, whereas the CPA license exists for the external attest work a CMA holder may not sign.
terms.whyItMatters: A corporate-finance roleplay asking which credential fits a cost-analyst career path needs this internal-versus-external split stated with its hour requirement.

terms.definition: A card, bin or electronic signal that authorizes replenishment only after downstream consumption, making it a PULL system — the opposite of material requirements planning, which PUSHES output on a forecast whether or not the next station has consumed the last batch.
terms.whyItMatters: Production questions test the pull-versus-push distinction directly: the signal-driven system builds only what was used, so it is the answer when the scenario complains of piled-up work in process.

terms.definition: Hear, empathize, apologize, resolve, diagnose — five steps whose last one is the whole difference: once the customer is satisfied the employee traces why the failure happened and reports it, converting a single complaint into a process fix. The four-step LAST script stops at resolve and generates no such feedback into the operation.
terms.whyItMatters: Hospitality roleplays about a failure that keeps recurring reward the competitor who closes the loop rather than just the ticket.

terms.definition: Brown and Levinson's term for any move that damages a hearer's public self-image - a criticism, a refusal, an order, a correction - together with the two repairs speakers use on it. Negative politeness protects the hearer's freedom by hedging and leaving an exit ('if you have a moment, could you possibly...'); positive politeness protects the hearer's need to be liked, using shared identity, praise and in-group language. Choosing the wrong repair is why a technically polite email still lands badly.
terms.whyItMatters: A supervisor roleplay that asks you to correct an employee's work is scored on which softening strategy you choose, not just on the accuracy of the correction.

terms.definition: Increased risk-taking AFTER an agreement is signed because someone else now bears the downside — an insured driver who stops locking the car, a bank lending recklessly while expecting a rescue. Adverse selection is the mirror problem BEFORE signing, when the riskiest applicants are the most eager buyers and the seller cannot tell them apart.
terms.whyItMatters: Items describing a party who behaves worse once protected are testing the before-versus-after timing that separates these two information problems; the timing is the whole answer.

terms.definition: The Hersey-Blanchard model matching four styles — directing, coaching, supporting, and delegating — to the follower's readiness, blending high or low task behavior with high or low relationship behavior; there is no single best style, which is what separates it from trait theories of leadership.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay pairing one veteran and one brand-new employee is scored on assigning a different named style to each and justifying it by readiness.

terms.definition: A court order directing an employer to withhold part of a worker's pay and send it to a creditor, capped by federal law as a share of disposable earnings.
terms.whyItMatters: It is the end point of the debt-control storyline in a personal-finance roleplay, and it reaches the paycheck without the debtor's consent.

terms.definition: Filters whole groups after aggregation, where WHERE filters individual rows before it: 'WHERE amount > 100' throws out small orders and then sums what remains, while 'HAVING SUM(amount) > 100' keeps every order and throws out customers whose total falls short. Run on the same table, the two return different customer lists.
terms.whyItMatters: A query item asks for customers whose yearly spend tops a threshold; putting the test in the WHERE clause returns the wrong set even though the query runs without error.

terms.definition: State-granted legal permission to perform work that is illegal without it — signing an audit opinion, selling securities, practicing law. A voluntary certification is issued by a private association instead, so losing it costs you the letters after your name but never the legal right to keep working.
terms.whyItMatters: A finance roleplay that asks what a new hire may and may not sign turns on this line: an unlicensed staff accountant can prepare the workpapers but cannot issue the opinion.

terms.definition: An organization-wide commitment to continuous improvement and quality.
terms.whyItMatters: A quality culture lowers defects and lifts loyalty over time.

terms.definition: An advance promise of a specific payout when a stated service standard is missed — the meal free after 30 minutes, the night comped on a late check-in — paid on the condition alone with no proof of loss and no argument. A warranty answers a product defect after the fact and requires a claim to be substantiated; this one is designed to be trivially easy to invoke.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges reward a competitor who proposes an unconditional, easy-to-claim guarantee for a service failure instead of extending a warranty that does not apply.

terms.definition: Something that happens between the balance-sheet date and the day statements are issued. ASC 855 splits them in two: if the underlying condition already existed at the balance-sheet date — a customer bankruptcy confirming a receivable was already bad — the statements are adjusted; if the condition arose afterward, such as a warehouse fire in January, it is disclosed only.
terms.whyItMatters: Year-end roleplays ask whether a January development changes December's reported numbers, and this recognized-versus-nonrecognized split is the whole answer.

terms.definition: The reasoning error of treating sequence as cause: sales rose after the new sign went up, therefore the sign raised sales. The test has two parts - could any other change explain the same movement (season, a competitor closing, a price cut, a general market lift), and is there a mechanism connecting the two? It is the fallacy behind most claimed advertising results, because campaigns are launched in the same weeks that demand naturally climbs.
terms.whyItMatters: A promotion roleplay that hands you a sales bump right after a campaign is scored on whether you ask for a control comparison instead of claiming the credit.

terms.definition: Focusing on producing the goods or services in which one has a comparative advantage.
terms.whyItMatters: Specialization improves efficiency and is the basis of trade.

terms.definition: Loan amount divided by the appraised value of the asset securing it; the higher it is, the less cushion a lender has and the more likely mortgage insurance is required.
terms.whyItMatters: Home-financing scenarios test why a larger down payment lowers the cost of borrowing, and this ratio is the mechanism.

terms.definition: A table containing little more than two foreign keys, plus any attribute that belongs to the pairing itself, which converts a single many-to-many relationship into two one-to-many relationships; without it a students-and-courses design has nowhere legal to record that one pair, since neither side's table has room for many values.
terms.whyItMatters: Database-design questions that describe products appearing in many orders and orders holding many products are testing whether you add this third table rather than repeating columns.

terms.definition: FINRA registration permitting an individual to sell general securities to the public, earned by passing the Securities Industry Essentials exam plus a top-off exam and requiring sponsorship by a member firm — a candidate cannot even sit for it unaffiliated. Charging a fee for advice rather than selling products requires a Series 65 or 66 instead.
terms.whyItMatters: A financial-services roleplay that asks what a new advisor may do on day one hinges on which registration is in place and who sponsored it.

terms.definition: Law developed through court decisions and legal precedents rather than legislation.
terms.whyItMatters: Many business principles, like contract formation, are rooted in common law.

terms.definition: A physical or software constraint that makes the wrong action impossible or immediately obvious — a plug that only fits one way, a field that refuses an invalid date — so defects are PREVENTED at the source, unlike statistical process control, which detects defects after they have already been produced.
terms.whyItMatters: Quality-method questions distinguish prevention from detection, and the mistake-proofing device is the accepted example of prevention when a scenario describes a repeated human error.

terms.term: Mail, Internet, or Telephone Order Merchandise Rule
terms.definition: An FTC rule under which a seller advertising no shipping date must ship within 30 days of a properly completed order, or send the buyer a revised date carrying the right to cancel for a prompt refund. Staying silent past the deadline obliges a refund whether or not the customer asks, so the clock runs against the seller by default.
terms.whyItMatters: An online-order complaint roleplay is decided by this clock, and the winning answer is a legal duty rather than a courtesy gesture.

terms.definition: The motion in Robert's Rules that closes debate and forces an immediate vote on the pending item. It is not the item itself and it is not a question: it must be seconded, is undebatable and unamendable, and takes a two-thirds vote because it strips members of the right to speak. Someone shouting 'Question!' from the floor has not made this motion and has not ended debate - the chair must still put it to the assembly.
terms.whyItMatters: A meeting-procedure item that shows a chair cutting off discussion on a simple majority is testing the two-thirds threshold attached to this motion.

terms.definition: Divide 70 by an annual growth rate written in whole percentage points to get the years a quantity needs to double: real output growing 3.5% a year doubles in 20 years, while 7% growth doubles it in 10 — so a one-point difference in growth is a decade of living standards.
terms.whyItMatters: Global-trade and economic-development items ask which of two developing markets a firm should enter first; the answer turns on doubling time, not on this year's growth number.

terms.definition: The total amount, including interest and fees, paid to borrow money.
terms.whyItMatters: Comparing the true cost of credit lets competitors judge whether borrowing is worthwhile.

terms.definition: Respecting and adapting to the values and practices of different cultures.
terms.whyItMatters: It lets a business serve diverse markets and build inclusive teams.

terms.definition: The balanced tree structure behind most database indexes: a lookup descends a few levels instead of reading every row, costing about log2(n) page reads — roughly 20 steps in a 1,000,000-row table where a full scan touches all 1,000,000. Doubling the table adds a single step, so an index worth little at 10,000 rows is worth enormously more at 10,000,000.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked why a customer lookup that was instant last year now takes 30 seconds, the competitor has to contrast logarithmic index cost with linear scan cost rather than blame the server.

terms.definition: Renewal credit a credentialed professional must earn on a fixed cycle to keep the credential active — most state boards require a CPA to report 120 hours across a rolling three-year period with a 20-hour annual floor plus a mandated ethics course, and unused hours lapse rather than carry forward. Unlike a degree, it has no completion point.
terms.whyItMatters: The finance roleplay that asks how an accountant stays qualified year to year wants the cycle and the hour count, not a sentence about lifelong learning.

terms.definition: A Pareto split of stock by annual dollar usage: roughly the top 20 percent of items carrying about 80 percent of the value are class A and get tight control and frequent counts, class B moderate control, class C the low-value bulk that is managed loosely with large buffers.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked how a warehouse manager should spend limited counting and control effort, the accepted answer is to classify by dollar usage and concentrate on class A rather than treat every item alike.

terms.definition: Federal rules under which gift card funds may not expire for at least 5 years from the date of the last load, and an inactivity fee may not be charged unless the card has gone unused for at least 12 months and then no more than once per month, with every fee disclosed on the card itself.
terms.whyItMatters: A retail service roleplay about a card the customer says has expired turns on whether the balance is still owed, and the numbers are the answer.

terms.definition: A member's assertion that the rules are being broken at this moment - a motion made out of order, debate wandering off the pending question, a vote miscounted. It may interrupt a speaker, requires no second, is not debatable, and is settled by the chair's ruling rather than a vote, though any two members may appeal that ruling to the assembly. It must be timely: raised after the offending action is complete, it is normally too late.
terms.whyItMatters: Chapter meetings and management roleplays run on a written agenda test whether you know which objections may interrupt a speaker and which must wait for the floor.

terms.definition: The function that recruits, develops, and manages employees to meet organizational goals.
terms.whyItMatters: HR decisions shape staffing quality, service delivery, and culture.

terms.definition: Actual real GDP minus potential real GDP, divided by potential and multiplied by 100. Actual output of $19.4 trillion against potential of $20 trillion is a gap of −3%, the recessionary case that pulls prices and hiring down; a positive gap signals an overheating economy.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-cycle questions give an actual and a potential output figure and expect the sign and the percentage, not the word 'slowdown'.

terms.definition: The principle that a dollar today is worth more than a dollar in the future because it can earn a return.
terms.whyItMatters: This concept justifies interest, discounting, and why saving early beats saving late.

terms.definition: The share of a table's rows a filter matches, taken as matching rows over total rows: 200 hits in 100,000 rows is 0.2% and the optimizer uses the index, while a filter matching 40,000 of those rows is unselective and a full scan wins, because chasing 40,000 index pointers back into the table costs more than reading the table once.
terms.whyItMatters: An item asks why adding an index on a two-value status column changed nothing; the fraction of rows matched, not the presence of the index, decides it.

terms.definition: Freedom from any relationship that would let a firm review its own work: Sarbanes-Oxley bars nine categories of non-audit service for an audit client, forces the lead partner off the engagement after five years, and imposes a one-year cooling-off period before an auditor may join that client as CFO or controller. Objectivity is a mindset; this is the enforceable rule set.
terms.whyItMatters: An accounting roleplay in which the audit firm is offered the client's bookkeeping work is decided by these prohibitions, not by whether the team feels unbiased.

terms.definition: A doctrine holding that one bottleneck sets the output of the whole system, worked through five focusing steps — identify the constraint, exploit it, subordinate everything else to it, elevate it with added capacity, then repeat because the constraint has moved — so improvement anywhere else adds inventory, not throughput.
terms.whyItMatters: When a production roleplay describes one slow station, the judge wants the constraint named and the rest of the line paced to it, not a blanket speed-up of every station.

terms.definition: The process of creating, communicating, and delivering value to customers.
terms.whyItMatters: This is the umbrella concept behind many cluster and roleplay decisions.

terms.definition: Support organized around closing each contact quickly and cheaply, measured on handle time and cost per contact, with no expectation the same employee ever sees that customer again. A relationship model assigns named ownership and is measured on lifetime value and retention, accepting longer contacts to win a larger share of future spend — the two sets of targets contradict each other if mixed.
terms.whyItMatters: Choosing the model is the first decision in a customer-strategy roleplay, because every metric the competitor then proposes has to follow from it.

terms.definition: Tufte's format for comparison: a grid of miniature charts sharing identical axes, identical scales and identical design, with exactly one variable changing from panel to panel - one region, one month or one product each. Holding the scale constant across every panel is the whole specification, and letting each panel auto-scale to its own data is the most common way the format is faked, because it destroys the comparison it exists to make.
terms.whyItMatters: A data-visualization task that hands you five years of sales across eight stores is scored on choosing this over one line chart with eight tangled series.

terms.definition: Money stock times the number of times each dollar is spent equals the price level times real output: M × V = P × Q. Restated in growth rates, %ΔM + %ΔV = %ΔP + %ΔQ, so with turnover steady and output rising 2%, an 8% jump in the money stock leaves about 6% inflation.
terms.whyItMatters: Interest-rate and inflation items ask what happens to prices when the central bank expands the money stock faster than the economy grows; this identity produces the number.

terms.definition: The total amount of tax a person or business legally owes to the government.
terms.whyItMatters: Tax liabilities affect take-home income and the real return on financial decisions.

terms.definition: Deliberately putting back the duplicated columns that normalization removed, trading write cost and update anomalies for read speed: one wide table answers a report with zero joins, but a customer who changes her surname must now be rewritten in every row that copied it, and any row missed is a silent contradiction.
terms.whyItMatters: A reporting-performance roleplay asks why the analytics table repeats the region name in a million rows; the defensible answer is the read-versus-write trade-off, not sloppy design.

terms.definition: Comparing a specific process against a reference standard — internal across a firm's own units, competitive against a direct rival, or functional against a best-in-class firm in any industry — and importing the practice, not merely noting the score difference.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items ask which benchmarking type fits a bank studying an airline's check-in speed, so the three categories have to be distinguishable.

terms.definition: Member-governed body that publishes a code of ethics, administers credentialing exams and sets practice standards for a field — the AICPA for accountants, SHRM for HR professionals. A labor union may cover overlapping workers but bargains collectively over wages and conditions; an association negotiates nothing and its only sanction is revoking the credential.
terms.whyItMatters: The accounting roleplay that asks what a professional organization does for a member is scored on services and enforcement, and confusing it with a union loses the item.

terms.definition: Scheduling deliveries to arrive as production consumes them so carrying cost and warehouse space approach zero; the explicit trade against safety-stock buffering is that it removes the cushion that absorbs a late supplier, so one disrupted shipment stops the line.
terms.whyItMatters: A supply-disruption roleplay wants both halves — the carrying-cost saving and the exposure it creates — because recommending it without naming the supplier-reliability requirement is what costs the point.

terms.definition: The merchant's rebuttal after a cardholder disputes a transaction with the issuing bank — compelling evidence such as delivery confirmation and the authorization record is filed inside the network's response window, commonly 30 days. Losing costs the sale plus a fee of roughly $15 to $100, and a dispute ratio approaching 1% of transactions drops the merchant into a network monitoring program.
terms.whyItMatters: A payments-dispute roleplay rewards the competitor who separates a chargeback from an ordinary refund and knows the evidence deadline is not negotiable.

terms.definition: The highest-ranking class of motion in Robert's Rules - adjourn, recess, raise a question of privilege, call for the orders of the day - urgent enough that it may be made while other business is pending and outranks every subsidiary motion. Because it does not relate to the pending question it is undebatable in most forms, and its rank is exactly why a motion to adjourn can be made while an amendment is on the floor but an amendment cannot be made while adjournment is.
terms.whyItMatters: Items that ask which motion may be made while another is still pending are testing the precedence ladder, and this class is its top rung.

terms.definition: The extra satisfaction gained from consuming one more unit, which declines as consumption rises — the second slice of pizza is worth less than the first. A consumer maximizes total satisfaction by spreading a budget until satisfaction per dollar is equal across goods: the marginal utility of A over the price of A equals the marginal utility of B over the price of B.
terms.whyItMatters: Consumer-spending items give utility figures and prices for two products and ask which the buyer purchases next; the per-dollar rule, not the raw utility number, decides it.

terms.definition: The threshold at which an omission or misstatement would change a reasonable user's decision. SEC Staff Accounting Bulletin No. 99 rejects any pure size rule: a five-percent-of-income screen may flag items, but a tiny error that flips a loss into a profit, hides a broken loan covenant, or lifts a bonus over its target is material no matter how small the dollars.
terms.whyItMatters: Ethics questions ask whether a deliberate but tiny misstatement is acceptable, and the qualitative half of this standard is why the answer is no.

terms.definition: The yearly cost of borrowing stated as a percentage that folds in interest plus required fees, so two loans quoted at the same interest rate can carry different borrowing costs.
terms.whyItMatters: Cost-of-credit questions on the finance exam ask which loan is cheaper, and the answer is the one with the lower APR, not the lower nominal interest rate.

terms.definition: Splitting one table's rows horizontally across several servers by a key, so four servers each carry about 25% of the rows and the system gains write capacity and room. Replication does the opposite — it copies 100% of the rows onto every server, buying read capacity and failover but not one byte of extra space.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay on a database that has outgrown its server asks which approach fixes it; recommending more copies of a table that no longer fits is the trap the judge is watching for.

terms.definition: Duty a broker-dealer owes to recommend products that fit a customer's stated objectives, raised in 2020 to a best-interest obligation requiring conflicts to be disclosed. It still stops short of the fiduciary standard a registered investment adviser owes under the Advisers Act of 1940, where the client's interest comes first continuously, not only at the moment of a recommendation.
terms.whyItMatters: A financial-advising roleplay about recommending a higher-commission fund turns on which of the two duties the professional is actually held to.

terms.definition: Available production time in a shift divided by customer units demanded in that shift — the pace demand dictates, which is set outside the factory, unlike cycle time, the pace the line actually achieves; a cycle time above it means the plant cannot keep up with orders.
terms.whyItMatters: Line-balancing items give shift minutes and a daily order quantity and ask how often a unit must come off the line; confusing the demand-set pace with the observed one flips the answer.

terms.definition: Any gap between what the customer expected and what was delivered, including delivery that met every internal specification — a technically perfect order arriving after a promised time has failed. A defect is a measurable breach of a standard the company set, so every defect is a failure while many failures pass every internal check, which is why complaint data can never be replaced by quality-control data.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where the operation insists nothing went wrong is won by naming this distinction before proposing the remedy.

terms.definition: A symbol, word, or phrase that identifies and distinguishes a business or product.
terms.whyItMatters: Brands are valuable assets; competitors must understand trademark protection and infringement.

terms.definition: A written instruction, issued the moment a company reasonably anticipates a dispute, that suspends every routine deletion schedule and directs named custodians to preserve emails, chat threads, drafts and text messages on the subject. The duty attaches before any complaint is filed, and letting an auto-delete rule keep running past that point is what converts ordinary records management into spoliation, exposing the company to an adverse-inference instruction at trial.
terms.whyItMatters: Digital-risk items that ask what an employee must do with a group chat once a customer threatens to sue are testing this duty and, above all, its trigger point.

terms.definition: −MPC ÷ (1 − MPC): with a marginal propensity to consume of 0.8 it is −4, one unit smaller in size than the 5 attached to direct spending and opposite in sign, because the first round of a tax cut is partly saved rather than spent. A $100 million tax cut therefore adds about $400 million to output, not $500 million.
terms.whyItMatters: Government-and-business items ask which stimulates output more per dollar, a tax cut or direct purchases; the sign and the one-unit gap are the whole answer.

terms.definition: Spreading investments across different assets to reduce overall risk.
terms.whyItMatters: Diversification is the standard answer to lowering investment risk in finance events.

terms.definition: The result that a distributed data store can hold at most two of three guarantees — consistency, availability, and tolerance of a network partition. Because a partition is a fact of networks rather than a design option, the live choice is only between the other two: refuse the read and stay correct, or answer it and risk handing back stale data.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked why a cloud inventory system showed two stores different stock counts during an outage, the competitor has to name the trade-off the vendor chose instead of calling it a bug.

terms.definition: Statement of the principles a profession owes the public, enforced by a licensing or membership board that can suspend or revoke the credential itself. A code of conduct is narrower and employer-issued: it lists prohibited acts and is enforced through progressive discipline up to termination, which ends the job but leaves the right to practice intact.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where an employee follows company policy yet violates a professional standard requires naming which body can act and what each can take away.

terms.definition: Maps five ways of handling a disagreement — competing, collaborating, compromising, avoiding and accommodating — on two axes: assertiveness, meaning concern for your own outcome, and cooperativeness, meaning concern for the other party's. Collaborating is high on both and costs the most time; compromising sits at the middle of both and splits the difference, so treating those two as synonyms is the classic wrong answer.
terms.whyItMatters: Conflict roleplays name a deadline, and the judge wants the mode matched to it — collaborate when the relationship and the outcome both matter and time exists, compromise when it does not.

terms.definition: Availability multiplied by performance multiplied by quality, each a percentage — so a machine running 90 percent uptime at 90 percent of rated speed with 90 percent good output scores about 73 percent, which is why the product exposes losses the three separate rates hide.
terms.whyItMatters: Equipment and maintenance questions ask why a line reported as 'ninety percent up' still misses its quota; multiplying the three loss categories is the accepted way to show it.

terms.definition: A privacy demand the business must first authenticate as coming from the consumer, then answer within 45 days, extendable once by a further 45 with notice, covering the categories collected in the preceding 12 months. It must be handled free of charge unless it is manifestly unfounded or excessive, and acting on it without verifying identity is itself a breach.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay where a caller demands their records deleted tests whether the competitor verifies identity before acting and can state the response clock.

terms.definition: The measured luminance relationship between text and the background behind it under the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, expressed from 1:1 to 21:1. Level AA requires at least 4.5:1 for body text and 3:1 for large text - 18 point, or 14 point bold - plus 3:1 for interface components and meaningful graphics; level AAA raises body text to 7:1. Light grey captions and a pale brand colour on a white slide are the two failures that show up most.
terms.whyItMatters: A written event or presentation judged on accessibility is scored on naming the threshold your deck actually meets, not on asserting that the colours look readable.

terms.definition: Raising purchases and taxes by the same dollar amount still lifts output by exactly that amount, because the spending multiplier 1 ÷ (1 − MPC) and the tax multiplier −MPC ÷ (1 − MPC) sum to 1. Spending and taxing $50 billion each adds $50 billion to GDP with no change in the deficit.
terms.whyItMatters: Fiscal items test whether a competitor thinks a deficit-neutral package does nothing; the arithmetic says its effect is positive and equal to the package.

terms.definition: What a deposit actually earns over a year once compounding is counted, which is why a savings account paying 5% compounded monthly returns more than 5%.
terms.whyItMatters: A savings-comparison roleplay hands the competitor two accounts with the same stated rate but different compounding periods; APY is the only figure that ranks them.

terms.definition: (All external recruiting costs + all internal recruiting costs) divided by the number of hires made in the same period — advertising, agency fees, travel, referral bonuses and recruiter salary all belong in the numerator, so $84,000 of total spend against 24 hires is $3,500. Only completed hires count in the denominator, never openings still in process.
terms.whyItMatters: A hiring-manager roleplay that asks you to justify a recruiting budget to an owner is scored on whether you divide total recruiting spend by hires rather than quoting the job-board invoice alone.

terms.definition: Keep three copies of the data on two different media types with one copy held off-site; the arithmetic is the whole point, because a single fire cannot reach the off-site copy, a single failing drive model cannot corrupt the second medium, and one ransomware blast radius cannot encrypt all three at once.
terms.whyItMatters: A storage roleplay about a flooded back office is graded on stating the counts, since answering 'we back up nightly' does not survive the follow-up about where the backup was sitting.

terms.definition: Statutory shield for an employee who reports suspected fraud: Sarbanes-Oxley gives a retaliation complaint 180 days to reach OSHA, while Dodd-Frank pays an SEC tipster 10% to 30% of sanctions when the recovery exceeds $1 million. Reporting internally first preserves the retaliation claim but is not a precondition of the SEC award.
terms.whyItMatters: In a business-ethics roleplay about a coworker's falsified expense reports, the graded answer names the channel and the filing window, not just 'tell someone'.

terms.definition: Continuous small improvements generated by the workers doing the job, accumulating gradually at near-zero capital cost — deliberately opposed to kaikaku or reengineering, which is a rare, top-down, capital-heavy redesign of the whole process.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay asks how to streamline work without a budget, the incremental frontline approach is the fitting recommendation, and the judge listens for why you did not propose a full redesign.

terms.definition: Under the Electronic Fund Transfer Act's implementing rule, a consumer has 60 days from the statement showing a disputed debit-card or ACH transfer to notify the bank; the bank then has 10 business days to investigate, or may extend to 45 calendar days only if it posts provisional credit inside those 10 days, and must report its findings within 3 business days of finishing. Liability for a lost card is capped at $50 when reported within 2 business days of discovery and $500 after that. Credit-card charges are excluded — those run on the Fair Credit Billing Act's two-billing-cycle track.
terms.whyItMatters: A financial-services or banking roleplay in which a client's debit card was drained overnight is scored on whether the competitor cites the 10-business-day investigation and the provisional-credit condition, instead of promising an immediate refund no associate can authorize.

terms.definition: Giving full attention, checking understanding, and responding thoughtfully to a speaker.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges expect competitors to handle questions and concerns clearly.

terms.definition: Value created by converting raw materials into a finished good a buyer actually wants — wheat into bread, bauxite into a can — as distinct from place utility (moving the good to where the buyer shops), time utility (having it on hand at the hour demand occurs), and possession utility (transferring ownership through payment terms); a redesign adds form utility, a faster truck does not.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays that ask how marketing adds value to a product are scored on naming which of the four utilities each activity creates and separating them; a general answer about 'adding value' loses the point.

terms.definition: One minus the share of each additional dollar of income that gets spent, so an MPC of 0.75 leaves 0.25. It is the multiplier's denominator: 1 ÷ 0.25 = 4, meaning the more households save out of a raise, the smaller the ripple from any injection of spending.
terms.whyItMatters: Consumer-spending questions give a change in income and a change in saving and expect the multiplier that follows, not a definition of thrift.

terms.definition: Total monthly debt payments divided by gross monthly income, the figure a lender uses to decide how much more a borrower can carry.
terms.whyItMatters: Loan-approval scenarios turn on this number, and competitors are expected to compute it from a client's payment list rather than judge the debt total by feel.

terms.definition: Striping with parity distributed across at least 3 disks: usable capacity is (n−1)/n of the raw total, so four 2 TB disks give 6 TB rather than 8, and exactly one disk may fail with no data lost. The exposure is the rebuild — a second failure while the array reconstructs the first destroys everything on it.
terms.whyItMatters: A storage-purchase roleplay asks how much of a quoted 8 TB array the business actually gets and how many drive failures it survives; both numbers come straight from the level.

terms.definition: Stretch of the calendar when insiders may not trade their own company's stock, typically closing two to four weeks before quarter-end and reopening one to two full trading days after earnings are released. A Rule 10b5-1 plan is the only clean way around it: trades are pre-scheduled and, under the 2023 amendments, cannot begin for at least 90 days.
terms.whyItMatters: A corporate-finance roleplay in which an employee wants to sell vested shares the week before an earnings release is answered by the window, not by intent.

terms.definition: Software that explodes a master production schedule through the bill of materials and nets it against on-hand stock to time component orders; it plans materials only, while enterprise resource planning extends the same database to finance, human resources and sales as one system.
terms.whyItMatters: Technology-in-operations items test whether you can scope the two acronyms apart — the narrow materials planner versus the company-wide platform — which is the discrimination most competitors get backwards.

terms.definition: A motivation model splitting job factors into hygiene factors — pay, supervision, working conditions, policy — whose absence causes dissatisfaction but whose presence never motivates, and motivators such as achievement, recognition, and responsibility, which alone produce satisfaction; the two run on separate scales rather than opposite ends of one.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items describe a raise that failed to lift engagement and expect the hygiene-versus-motivator distinction as the explanation.

terms.definition: Links internal service quality to employee satisfaction and retention, then to productivity and delivered value, then to customer loyalty and finally revenue growth. The practical claim is that the cheapest lever on the customer end of the chain usually sits at the employee end, so a loyalty problem is often a scheduling or training problem.
terms.whyItMatters: Backs a roleplay recommendation to fix rostering or training when the case presents falling guest satisfaction as the problem.

terms.definition: A readability score that converts a passage into a U.S. school grade: 0.39 x (total words / total sentences) + 11.8 x (total syllables / total words) - 15.59. Because sentence length is multiplied by 0.39 and syllable count by 11.8, swapping 'utilize' for 'use' moves the score less than splitting one 30-word sentence into two 15-word ones; consumer-facing documents are normally targeted at grade 8 or below.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay that asks you to rewrite a return policy for shoppers is scored on whether you can name a measurable target and the two levers that hit it, instead of promising to 'make it simpler.'

terms.definition: Employed people divided by the civilian working-age population — the denominator counts everyone of working age, including those not looking for work. With 155 million employed out of 260 million, the ratio is 59.6%; the jobless rate uses the labor force instead and can fall simply because searchers quit looking.
terms.whyItMatters: Unemployment-rate items pair a falling jobless rate with a falling employment share and ask which one shows the labor market actually improving.

terms.definition: An institution such as a bank, credit union, or brokerage that offers money-management products.
terms.whyItMatters: Choosing the right provider is a recurring judgment in personal-finance scenarios.

terms.definition: Mirrored pairs that are then striped: usable capacity is exactly half the raw total, so the same four 2 TB disks give 4 TB instead of 6, but the array survives one failure in every pair and rebuilds by copying a single disk rather than recomputing parity from all the rest.
terms.whyItMatters: Comparing two quotes for the same four drives, the competitor has to trade 2 TB of capacity against a faster, safer rebuild — a judge expects the capacity figure said out loud.

terms.definition: Choosing among permissible accounting options — timing a shipment, trimming a reserve, deferring maintenance — to steer reported income toward a target while staying technically inside GAAP. That technical legality is what separates it from outright fraud, and why the ethical question becomes one of intent and disclosure rather than rule-breaking.
terms.whyItMatters: Ethics prompts describe a manager pushing December orders out the door to hit a quarterly number and ask whether anything wrong happened even though no rule was broken.

terms.definition: Flat daily travel allowance that substitutes for itemized receipts — the federal standard for the continental U.S. runs near $110 for lodging plus $68 for meals and incidentals, with the first and last travel days paid at 75% of the meal portion. Anything paid above the published rate becomes taxable wages to the traveler.
terms.whyItMatters: A hospitality or sales roleplay budgeting a three-day trip needs the arithmetic: two full days at the meal rate plus two partial days at three quarters of it.

terms.definition: A five-step workplace discipline — sort out what is not needed, set remaining items in fixed marked locations, shine and inspect, standardize the arrangement in writing, and sustain it by audit — where the fifth step is the one that fails and turns the program into a one-time cleanup.
terms.whyItMatters: Safety and efficiency roleplays reward naming a structured method for a cluttered work area rather than saying 'organize it,' and the sustain-by-audit step is the detail that separates a full answer.

terms.term: Fair Credit Billing Act billing-error window
terms.definition: A credit-card holder must dispute a charge in writing within 60 days of the statement date on which it first appeared; the issuer then has 30 days to acknowledge the notice and two complete billing cycles — never more than 90 days — to resolve it, and may not report the disputed amount as delinquent while the claim is open. It reaches open-end credit only, so the same $400 charge disputed on a debit card is handled instead under Regulation E's 10-business-day investigation.
terms.whyItMatters: Business-law and finance exam items pair this window against the debit-card rule, and a customer-complaint roleplay about a double-billed credit-card charge expects the competitor to state the 60-day filing deadline before offering any goodwill.

terms.definition: A letter layout in which every element - date, inside address, salutation, body, complimentary close and signature block - begins flush at the left margin with no indentation, set on one-inch margins with a blank line between parts and no blank-line indents inside paragraphs. Modified block, its near neighbour, moves the date and the closing to start at the horizontal center of the page; semi-block does that and also indents the first line of each paragraph.
terms.whyItMatters: Formatting items on the exam give you the same letter three ways and ask which is full block, and written-event submissions lose presentation points for mixing two of the three.

terms.definition: Revenue equals the rate times the taxable base, and the base itself shrinks as the rate climbs, so collections are zero at a 0% rate and zero again at 100% and peak somewhere between. Above that peak a rate cut raises revenue; below it — where most real systems sit — a cut still loses money.
terms.whyItMatters: Tax questions ask whether cutting a rate can raise collections; credit goes to the competitor who names which side of the peak the rate has to be on.

terms.definition: Governs contracts for the sale of goods — movable, tangible items — and displaces common-law contract rules for them, so services, employment and real estate stay under common law. Its section 2-207 is the sharpest break: a definite acceptance forms a contract even when it adds terms, where the common-law mirror-image rule would have turned the same reply into a counteroffer.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam fact patterns about a purchase order with extra terms typed on the back are decided first by asking whether goods or services were sold.

terms.definition: Balances owed divided by total available revolving credit, weighted heavily in a credit score and generally kept under 30% to avoid a penalty.
terms.whyItMatters: Credit-score advising roleplays reward the competitor who tells a client to pay down balances or raise a limit instead of closing an unused card.

terms.definition: Written with dollar signs as $A$1, it pins both the column and the row so the address does not shift when the formula is copied down or across; a relative reference such as A1 moves with the copy, and a mixed reference such as $A1 or A$1 freezes only the half carrying the dollar sign.
terms.whyItMatters: Spreadsheet items give a tax rate in one cell and ask why copying the formula produced zeros further down the column; the missing dollar signs are the graded answer.

terms.definition: Dollar ceiling below which accepting a business courtesy is not treated as influence — federal ethics rules cap it at $20 per occasion and $50 per source per year, and many corporate policies copy those figures. Above the line the item must be refused, returned, or reported, and splitting one gift across two occasions is itself the violation.
terms.whyItMatters: A purchasing roleplay where a vendor sends playoff tickets is scored on whether the competitor applies the stated dollar limit and the reporting step.

terms.definition: A dependency network that estimates each task's expected duration as optimistic plus four times most likely plus pessimistic, divided by six — a weighted three-point estimate for work with uncertain durations, unlike a critical path calculation, which assumes one fixed duration per task.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items hand you three time estimates for a task and ask for the expected duration; the weighted formula, not a plain average of the three numbers, is the scored answer.

terms.definition: Sessions a virtual agent closes without handing the customer to a live representative, divided by every session that virtual agent opened — a bot that finishes 700 of 1,000 chats and passes 300 along contains 70%. The denominator is bot sessions only, which is what separates it from a self-service deflection rate measured against total support demand, so a bot nobody reaches can post a high containment figure while deflecting almost nothing.
terms.whyItMatters: A customer-service management roleplay that asks a competitor to justify a chatbot's return turns on this pair of denominators; quoting containment as though it were deflection overstates the labor saved and a judge listening for cost per contact will catch it.

terms.definition: Divides what is known about a person into four panes by crossing known-to-self against known-to-others: open, blind, hidden and unknown. Asking for feedback shrinks the blind pane, while voluntary self-disclosure shrinks the hidden pane — the two moves are not interchangeable, and only the first can surface a habit you cannot see in yourself.
terms.whyItMatters: A written item asking which pane a manager reduces by running a 360-degree review, and roleplays that ask a competitor to assess personal strengths and weaknesses, both depend on separating feedback from disclosure.

terms.definition: A formal written message with a clear subject, correct grammar, and appropriate tone.
terms.whyItMatters: Written events reward mastery of email conventions.

terms.definition: The split of a per-unit levy between buyer and seller, fixed by relative elasticities rather than by who writes the check: buyers absorb the fraction Es ÷ (Es + Ed). With supply elasticity 2 and demand elasticity 1, buyers carry two-thirds of a $3 tax as a $2 price rise and the seller nets $1 less.
terms.whyItMatters: Taxation items name the party legally charged and then ask who actually pays; the elasticity ratio, not the statute, decides.

terms.definition: A financial statement reporting the cash flowing into and out of a business over a period.
terms.whyItMatters: Cash flow reveals whether a business can pay its bills even when it reports a profit.

terms.definition: The bit count of a cryptographic key, which cannot be compared across algorithm families: a 256-bit symmetric key doubles in strength with each added bit, while a 2048-bit RSA key rests on the difficulty of factoring and rates at only about 112 bits of equivalent strength. The far bigger number is the weaker key.
terms.whyItMatters: A vendor-security roleplay asks whether a supplier advertising 2048-bit encryption beats one advertising 256-bit; reading the digits alone gives the wrong recommendation.

terms.definition: Post-employment restriction barring a departing worker from joining a competitor for a stated period and geography, commonly 6 to 12 months. Enforceability is a state question — California voids them outright and several states exempt hourly workers below a wage threshold — and a court will usually narrow an unreasonable radius rather than rewrite the deal.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay advising an employee who has an offer from a rival turns on this clause's scope and on whether the state will enforce it at all.

terms.definition: The process of finding and attracting qualified candidates for open positions.
terms.whyItMatters: Effective recruitment ensures a business has the talent to meet its needs.

terms.definition: A horizontal bar timeline showing each task's start, duration and overlap against calendar dates; it displays schedule but not logic, whereas a PERT network draws the dependency arrows that reveal which tasks actually control the finish date.
terms.whyItMatters: Project-management roleplays ask which tool to bring to a status meeting: the bar timeline communicates progress to a client, but it cannot answer which delay pushes the deadline.

terms.definition: A concession — a discount, a credit, or a downgrade to a cheaper plan — put in front of a customer at the moment they state an intent to cancel, and priced by a margin test: the ceiling is the gross margin still expected over the account's remaining tenure minus what winning that customer back would cost, so a 30% discount on a subscription carrying a 25% gross margin destroys value even though the account is retained. It is offered before cancellation is processed, unlike a win-back campaign, which targets customers who have already gone.
terms.whyItMatters: A retention roleplay that hands a competitor a cancelling account expects the concession to be defended with the account's remaining margin and acquisition cost, not with the largest discount the associate is allowed to give.

terms.definition: An arrangement that puts the main idea, request or answer in the very first sentence and places explanation after it - correct for routine requests, good news, and most internal messages, and expected by busy or senior readers. The indirect pattern reverses that into four ordered parts: a neutral buffer, the reasons, the bad news itself stated once, and a goodwill close. Choose by predicted reaction, not by topic: a refusal a reader already expects can still be written directly.
terms.whyItMatters: The most common written-event error is burying a recommendation in paragraph three of a message the reader will happily agree with.

terms.definition: Add the annual inflation rate to the unemployment rate: 6% price growth plus 5% joblessness scores 11. The two are weighted equally, so a policy that trades two points of inflation for one point of employment worsens the score even when the jobs number improves.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about consumer confidence and discretionary spending hand you both rates; the combined figure is what explains why traffic fell.

terms.definition: A shortcut that estimates how many years an investment takes to double by dividing 72 by the annual percentage return.
terms.whyItMatters: Investing roleplays reward a competitor who can tell a client on the spot that 8% doubles their money in about nine years.

terms.definition: Intangible activities that satisfy customer needs and wants.
terms.whyItMatters: Services require different quality, staffing, and marketing choices than goods.

terms.definition: Two different inputs producing the same fixed-length digest, which has to be possible because inputs are unlimited and digests are not. A 256-bit digest has 2^256 possible outputs, but the birthday bound puts an attacker's expected work at about 2^128 attempts — the square root, not the full space — which is why a 128-bit digest is retired and a 256-bit one is not.
terms.whyItMatters: An information-ethics item asks why a system that stores digests instead of files can still be attacked; the square-root shortcut, not the digest length on the label, is the reasoning.

terms.definition: Reimbursement arrangement that keeps expense payments out of taxable wages, valid only when the expense has a business connection, is substantiated with receipts within 60 days, and any excess advance is returned within 120 days. Miss any one of the three and the arrangement is non-accountable, so every reimbursed dollar is added to the W-2 and taxed as pay.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam item on a sales rep who never turns in travel receipts is really asking why the reimbursement showed up as taxable income.

terms.definition: Summing durations along every dependency chain and taking the longest one as the shortest possible project duration; every task on it has zero float, so any slip there slips the whole project, while a delay off it is absorbed.
terms.whyItMatters: A project roleplay that asks which of several late tasks to escalate is answered by locating the zero-float chain, because effort spent on the others buys no finish-date improvement.

terms.definition: Contacts an agent passes to another agent or queue, divided by contacts that agent handled — 40 hand-offs across 500 calls is 8%.
