It counts lateral moves to a peer at the same authority level, whereas an escalation rate counts only contacts pushed up to a supervisor or a higher support tier, so a caller routed sideways to a billing specialist raises this figure and leaves escalation untouched. Every transfer also breaks first contact resolution, even when the second agent solves the issue on the same call.
terms.whyItMatters: In a contact-center roleplay judged on resolving service situations, a competitor proposing skills-based routing has to say which of the two ratios the change should move, since routing callers correctly the first time cuts transfers without touching escalations.

terms.definition: A five-step persuasive outline - attention, need, satisfaction, visualization, action - where the fourth step is the one that distinguishes it: the audience is walked through a vivid picture of life after adopting the proposal (or of life if they refuse) before any request is made. A plain problem-solution outline stops after satisfaction, and a call to action without the visualization step is the most common way competitors flatten it back into three parts.
terms.whyItMatters: When a roleplay asks you to sell a manager on a new procedure, this sequence gives a scored structure; naming the five steps beats an unstructured pitch every time.

terms.definition: Vroom's model that motivational force equals expectancy times instrumentality times valence — belief effort produces performance, belief performance produces the reward, and the value placed on that reward — so a zero on any one factor drives the whole product to zero regardless of the other two.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items describe an incentive nobody chases and expect you to name which of the three multiplied factors is missing, since the multiplication is the tested part.

terms.definition: Nominal rate multiplied by the ratio of home prices to foreign prices, which is what decides whether exporting is actually cheaper. A 10% currency fall paired with 10% more home inflation than abroad leaves this measure unchanged, so the apparent export advantage is worth nothing.
terms.whyItMatters: Global-trade roleplays hand you a currency move and an inflation gap and ask whether the firm's goods really got cheaper overseas.

terms.definition: The rate applied to the next dollar earned, which is the top bracket a taxpayer reaches rather than the rate paid on all of their income.
terms.whyItMatters: Tax-liability items test whether a raise into a higher bracket taxes the whole salary at the new rate — it does not, only the dollars above the bracket line.

terms.definition: A primary key spread across two or more columns, where uniqueness is broken only when every column in the key matches at once — a key on (student_id, course_id) lets the same student appear 6 times and the same course appear 300 times, but the pair exactly once.
terms.whyItMatters: Enrollment and order-line questions ask how many rows one student or one product may hold; the count comes from reading the columns in the key, not from any rule about the table.

terms.definition: Withholding certificate an employee files so the employer deducts the right federal income tax; the 2020 redesign dropped allowances for a five-step worksheet stated in dollars, including $2,000 per qualifying child. It is not Form I-9, which proves work authorization within three business days of hire, nor Form W-9, which an independent contractor files instead.
terms.whyItMatters: A first-day onboarding roleplay is scored on knowing which of the three forms does what, since a competitor who names the wrong one has the new hire unpaid or unauthorized.

terms.definition: A deliverable-oriented decomposition of a project into progressively smaller work packages governed by the 100 percent rule — the children of any element must sum to exactly that element, no more and no less — so it captures scope, not sequence, which the schedule adds afterward.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked how to start planning a project, the accepted first move is decomposing deliverables before estimating or scheduling, and the completeness rule is what stops forgotten work becoming a budget overrun.

terms.definition: The clean verdict an independent auditor issues when statements are fairly presented in all material respects — a conclusion about conformity with the reporting framework, not a guarantee of accuracy or solvency. It ranks above a qualified opinion, which carries one bounded exception, an adverse opinion, which says the statements are materially misstated, and a disclaimer, where the auditor could not gather enough evidence to conclude at all.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items quote an audit report and ask what a lender may safely conclude from that specific wording.

terms.definition: Section 102(c) of the Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act forbids conditioning a written warranty on the buyer's use of a branded part or an authorized service center unless the warrantor supplies that part or service free of charge or holds an FTC waiver — so an independent repair shop cannot by itself void coverage, and neither can failing to mail back a registration card, because the purchase date is what proves the claim. A service contract sold for separate consideration is not a warranty and never falls under this rule.
terms.whyItMatters: An automotive- or electronics-services roleplay where a guest was told their warranty died because they used an outside mechanic is scored on interpreting the policy correctly to the customer rather than repeating the store's line.

terms.definition: A formal document in standard format used for official outside communication.
terms.whyItMatters: Judges expect correct formatting, tone, and structure.

terms.definition: Price of one currency in another, derived from each one's quote against a third: if $1 buys €0.90 and $1 buys £0.80, then €1 buys £0.889, since 0.80 ÷ 0.90 = 0.889. Any quoted pair that disagrees with that division is an arbitrage opportunity, which is why the three quotes stay consistent.
terms.whyItMatters: Exchange-rate items quote two currencies against the dollar and ask what a euro invoice costs a British subsidiary — a division, not a lookup.

terms.definition: A financial statement showing a business's assets, liabilities, and equity at a single point in time.
terms.whyItMatters: The balance sheet is where competitors read financial position and solvency.

terms.definition: A precomputed lookup of billions of password-to-digest pairs that reverses an unprotected stored password in seconds. Adding a distinct random value to each record before hashing defeats it by arithmetic rather than by secrecy: the attacker must now build one table per record, so 1,000,000 stored passwords demand 1,000,000 tables instead of the single shared one.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked why one breached company's passwords were readable overnight and another's were not, the competitor has to explain the per-record work multiplier, not just say the second one 'used encryption'.

terms.definition: Requires certain agreements to be evidenced by a signed writing before a court will enforce them: sales of land, promises that cannot be performed within one year, promises to answer for another party's debt, agreements made in consideration of marriage, executor promises, and sales of goods priced at $500 or more under UCC section 2-201. A covered oral deal is not void — it is unenforceable if the other side raises the defense.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplay judges ask which handshake commitments a manager can still rely on, and the $500 goods figure and the one-year rule are what settle it.

terms.definition: Narrower post-employment restriction that lets a departing worker take any job but forbids contacting the former employer's customers or recruiting its staff, usually for 12 to 24 months. Because it limits whom you may approach rather than where you may work, courts enforce it in states that will not enforce a non-compete at all.
terms.whyItMatters: A sales-management roleplay about a rep who leaves and calls his old book of business is decided by this clause, not by the broader competition ban.

terms.definition: Latest allowable start minus earliest possible start for a task — the delay it can absorb before the project finish moves; total float is shared along a chain, whereas free float is the smaller amount that delays no immediately following task at all.
terms.whyItMatters: Given a network with early and late start dates, exam questions ask how long a task can slip; confusing the shared allowance with the task-level one over-promises the client in a status roleplay.

terms.definition: The activities a business uses to build satisfaction, trust, and loyalty.
terms.whyItMatters: Strong customer relations support repeat business and reputation.

terms.definition: An argument broken into six named parts: the claim, the grounds (the data offered), the warrant - the usually unstated assumption that licenses moving from the grounds to the claim - plus backing that supports the warrant, a qualifier that limits how strongly the claim holds, and a rebuttal that names the conditions under which it fails. Arguments collapse at the warrant far more often than at the data, because the missing piece was never said aloud.
terms.whyItMatters: Defending a recommendation to a judge who pushes back means naming the assumption connecting your figures to your conclusion, which is the step competitors skip when they simply repeat the data louder.

terms.definition: Export price index divided by import price index, times 100. A country whose export prices climb 6% while import prices climb 2% moves from 100 to about 104 and can buy more foreign goods per unit shipped; a commodity exporter watching prices slide sees the figure drop even with export volume flat.
terms.whyItMatters: Trade-alliance and global-environment questions ask who gained from a shift in world prices, and the ratio of the two indexes settles it.

terms.definition: Techniques to address disagreements and reach mutually acceptable solutions.
terms.whyItMatters: Strong conflict resolution keeps teams cohesive and prevents escalation.

terms.definition: Total tax paid divided by total income, always lower than the top bracket a taxpayer falls in because earlier dollars were taxed at lower rates.
terms.whyItMatters: A finance exam item gives income and tax owed and asks for the rate actually paid; answering with the bracket rate is the trap.

terms.definition: An independent report on whether a service provider's controls actually operated across an observation window, normally 3 to 12 months of collected evidence. A Type I examines the same controls on one single date and attests only that they were designed correctly — so a vendor holding only a Type I has never had those controls tested over time.
terms.whyItMatters: A vendor-selection roleplay puts two cloud providers side by side, one with each report; the observation period is the distinction a judge scores.

terms.definition: State or city rule requiring an employer to publish a good-faith salary range inside the job posting itself, as Colorado's Equal Pay for Equal Work Act and New York City's Local Law 32 do. It attacks the gap at the offer stage, whereas the Equal Pay Act of 1963 works after the fact by requiring equal pay for substantially equal work.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay preparing a competitor to negotiate an offer changes completely when the posted range is public, because the anchor is set before the conversation.

terms.definition: Comparing budgeted cost of work actually completed against what was spent and what was planned: cost performance index is earned value divided by actual cost, schedule performance index is earned value divided by planned value, and any index below 1.0 signals over budget or behind schedule.
terms.whyItMatters: Project-evaluation items ask whether a project that has spent sixty percent of its budget is in trouble; only the ratio against work completed answers it, and a raw spending percentage does not.

terms.definition: The total profit a business expects from a customer over the whole relationship.
terms.whyItMatters: CLV guides how much to invest in retention and service.

terms.definition: Calendar days from the day a requisition is approved to the day a candidate accepts the offer, averaged across openings. Its near-twin, time to hire, starts the clock later — at the day the hired person first applied — so time to fill measures the whole requisition including sourcing delay while time to hire measures only the candidate's own journey, and a 62-day time to fill can sit on top of a 19-day time to hire.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items give you both numbers and ask which one proves the bottleneck is job-posting approval rather than the interview loop.

terms.definition: Tufte's distortion metric: the size of the effect shown in the graphic divided by the size of the effect in the data, where an honest chart lands between 0.95 and 1.05. A 20 percent rise drawn as a bar twice as tall scores 5; scaling a pictogram by both height and width doubles a doubling into a fourfold area, scoring about 2. A truncated vertical axis inflates it the same way, which is why a bar chart's axis must start at zero even when a line chart's need not.
terms.whyItMatters: Data-visualization items give a chart and ask why it misleads, and the scored answer names the exaggeration, not just 'the graph looks unfair.'

terms.definition: A fixed list of goods and quantities repriced each period; this period's cost divided by the base period's cost, times 100, is the index. A $2,400 basket against a $2,000 base year prints 120, meaning prices are 20% above base — and because the quantities never change, substitution toward cheaper goods is invisible and the index overstates the true rise.
terms.whyItMatters: Inflation-impact questions ask a competitor to compute an index from two years of basket costs and then explain why the printed rate overstates what shoppers actually pay.

terms.definition: A financial statement showing revenue, expenses, and profit over a period of time.
terms.whyItMatters: It is the primary tool for judging whether operations are profitable.

terms.definition: Combines two tables and keeps only the rows matching on the join column, silently discarding unmatched rows from both sides — 500 customers joined to an orders table returns nothing at all for the 120 who have never ordered, so a customer count taken after the join reports 380 rather than 500.
terms.whyItMatters: A data-analysis item asks why a mailing list built from a joined query is short by exactly the number of inactive customers; the join type is the entire answer.

terms.definition: Employment clause transferring to the employer any invention conceived during the job, reaching further than copyright's work-made-for-hire rule because it also captures patents. Statutes such as California Labor Code section 2870 carve out inventions developed entirely on the worker's own time, without company equipment or trade secrets, and unrelated to the employer's business.
terms.whyItMatters: An entrepreneurship roleplay about a side project built after hours is scored on whether the competitor can state the carve-out's three conditions.

terms.definition: Value added by making ownership transferable — credit terms, layaway, financing, leasing, the transaction mechanics themselves — rather than by making the good (form utility), delivering it to the buyer's location (place utility), or holding it until demand appears (time utility); a dealer that adds 60-month zero-interest financing changes the product's form, place, and time not at all.
terms.whyItMatters: Hospitality and finance roleplays that ask you to justify offering a payment plan want the answer framed as a marketing utility the firm creates, not as a favor to the customer.

terms.definition: Inspecting a randomly drawn sample from a delivered lot and accepting or rejecting the entire lot on the count of defects found, against a stated acceptable quality level — the highest defect percentage treated as satisfactory — which trades a known risk of passing a bad lot for the cost of inspecting every unit.
terms.whyItMatters: Receiving-process questions ask how a buyer verifies a large shipment economically; naming the tolerable defect percentage and the risk it accepts is what distinguishes a full answer from 'check some of them'.

terms.definition: A relationship of mutual understanding and trust between a business and its customers.
terms.whyItMatters: Building rapport raises trust and the odds of repeat business.

terms.definition: Interference produced by the message's own words - unfamiliar jargon, an ambiguous pronoun, a term whose connotation differs for sender and receiver - as opposed to physical noise, which is external to the message (a loud room, a dropped call, small type), and psychological noise, which is inside the receiver (anxiety, distraction, a prior grudge). The distinction decides the fix: repeating the sentence louder cures only the physical kind.
terms.whyItMatters: An exam scenario where a customer misreads a policy term is a semantic-noise item, and the scored remedy is rewording, not resending.

terms.definition: The forward premium on a currency has to equal the gap between the two countries' interest rates, or borrowing in one and lending in the other earns a riskless profit. A 5% domestic rate against 2% abroad implies the foreign currency trades forward about 3% above spot, which cancels the yield advantage exactly.
terms.whyItMatters: International-finance items ask why a competitor should not simply park cash in the highest-yielding currency; the forward discount is the answer.

terms.definition: An amount subtracted directly from tax owed, so it is worth its full face value — unlike a deduction, which only reduces the income the tax is figured on.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items pair a $1,000 credit with a $1,000 deduction and ask which saves more; the credit does, by the taxpayer's bracket rate.

terms.definition: Building several internally consistent stories of how key uncertainties could resolve and stress-testing the strategy against each, rather than extending one forecast line; the output is a set of trigger points and prepared responses, not a single most-likely number.
terms.whyItMatters: Management written events on planning under uncertainty are graded on producing multiple plausible futures with named triggers, which a sales forecast alone does not supply.

terms.definition: A state privacy law binding a for-profit business only once it crosses one of three thresholds: more than $25 million in annual gross revenue, personal information on 100,000 or more California consumers or households, or at least 50% of revenue earned from selling or sharing that information. A small firm holding California data can sit entirely outside it.
terms.whyItMatters: A legal-issues item asks whether a startup with 4,000 California customers and $2 million in revenue must honor deletion requests; only the thresholds answer it.

terms.definition: Paid notice period during which a resigning employee stays on payroll but is kept away from the office, from clients and from starting at a competitor, commonly one to six months. It is enforceable in places that void a bare non-compete precisely because the employer keeps paying — the restraint is bought rather than merely imposed.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay advising a senior manager on a competitor's offer must separate this paid restriction from an unpaid non-compete, because only one keeps income flowing.

terms.definition: Charting sample measurements over time against limits computed from the process's own variation to separate common-cause noise from assignable-cause shifts; it monitors a process while it runs, unlike acceptance sampling, which judges a finished lot after the fact.
terms.whyItMatters: Quality-method roleplays ask how to catch a drifting machine before it produces scrap; watching the charted trend is the in-process answer, and inspecting finished goods is the one judges mark as too late.

terms.definition: Contacts fully resolved on the first interaction divided by total contacts handled — 1,200 of 1,500 is 80%. A case that is transferred to a second agent or reopened later counts as a failure even if it is solved the same day, which is why it moves in the opposite direction from average handle time whenever agents rush callers off the line.
terms.whyItMatters: In a contact-center roleplay judged on service improvement, the fix a competitor proposes has to raise this number; trimming call length by promising a callback lowers it.

terms.definition: Visual tools such as charts and diagrams that reinforce a message.
terms.whyItMatters: Competitors must select and justify aids that support their analysis.

terms.definition: The five-component model regulators and auditors use to evaluate controls — control environment, risk assessment, control activities, information and communication, and monitoring — and the benchmark against which management's Sarbanes-Oxley Section 404 assessment is judged. It supplies the structure; any single safeguard, such as splitting custody from recordkeeping, sits inside just one of the five.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays asking a manager to evaluate a store's controls expect the five components as the outline of the answer, not a scattered list of fixes.

terms.definition: Share of each extra dollar of income that leaves the country for foreign goods. It enters the multiplier as a leakage, turning 1 ÷ (1 − MPC) into 1 ÷ (1 − MPC + MPI): with MPC 0.8 the closed figure of 5 falls to 1 ÷ (0.2 + 0.1) = 3.33 once a tenth of new income is spent abroad.
terms.whyItMatters: Globalization questions ask why a stimulus works less well in a highly open economy; the leakage in the denominator is the mechanism.

terms.definition: Profit from selling an asset for more than its purchase price, taxable only once the sale happens and taxed at a lower rate when the asset was held over a year.
terms.whyItMatters: Investment scenarios ask whether a client owes tax on a stock that has risen in value; unrealized gains are not taxed until sold.

terms.definition: The legally fixed span between learning of a personal-data breach and having to report it — 72 hours to the supervising authority under EU rules, with U.S. state statutes commonly allowing 30 to 60 days for notice to the individuals affected. The clock starts at awareness, not at the intrusion, so an attack that sat undetected for 8 months still leaves the full window intact once it is found.
terms.whyItMatters: An incident roleplay asks when the company is late; competitors who count from the intrusion date report the firm as months overdue when it is in fact on day one.

terms.definition: Department of Labor-registered training program pairing paid on-the-job hours — about 2,000 a year under a journey-worker mentor — with at least 144 hours of related classroom instruction and scheduled wage increases as each skill is certified. An internship carries no registered hour floor, no mentor requirement and no guaranteed wage progression.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay on ways to gain real work experience is scored on naming the structured, paid, credentialed route rather than only the summer internship.

terms.definition: Unloading inbound freight and transferring it directly to outbound trailers within hours, sorting by destination on the dock, so the goods are never put away — the opposite of conventional warehousing, which stores, picks and holds stock and therefore incurs carrying cost that this eliminates.
terms.whyItMatters: Distribution roleplays about cutting inventory cost and speeding delivery expect this as the named technique, and the judge wants the requirement that inbound and outbound schedules be tightly synchronized.

terms.definition: Enforces a promise that never had a bargained-for exchange behind it when four elements line up: a clear and definite promise, the promisor's reasonable expectation that it would induce reliance, actual detrimental reliance by the promisee, and injustice avoidable only by enforcement. Recovery is usually capped at what reliance cost, not the full expectancy a consideration-backed contract would deliver.
terms.whyItMatters: Contract exam items about a supplier who withdrew a quoted price after the buyer already used it to bid a job test this doctrine, not consideration.

terms.definition: Talk time plus hold time plus after-call work, divided by contacts handled — 6 minutes of talk, 1 minute of hold and 3 minutes of wrap-up across 40 calls averages 10 minutes. Leaving wrap-up out of the numerator is the standard error, and it makes every staffing model built on the figure understaff the queue.
terms.whyItMatters: Staffing math in a peak-demand hospitality or call-center roleplay starts here, and exam items expect the wrap-up term to be inside the average.

terms.definition: Edward Hall's study of how people use physical distance, mapped to four zones: intimate from contact to about 18 inches, personal from 18 inches to 4 feet, social from 4 to 12 feet, and public beyond 12 feet. Normal business is transacted in the social zone, so a salesperson who closes to 3 feet has entered personal space and is read as pressure rather than warmth. The distances themselves are cultural, and the same 3 feet reads as ordinary in much of Latin America and as intrusive in northern Europe.
terms.whyItMatters: Nonverbal-cue items describe a customer stepping back during a demonstration, and the scored answer names the zone violation instead of calling it 'being uncomfortable.'

terms.definition: Splits output growth into three addends — the contribution of added capital, the contribution of added hours, and the residual left over. If output rises 4% while capital and labor together explain 2.5%, the remaining 1.5% is productivity growth, the only piece that raises income per worker permanently.
terms.whyItMatters: Productivity items ask a competitor to separate growth that came from hiring more people from growth that came from each worker producing more.

terms.definition: How easily an asset can be converted to cash without losing much value.
terms.whyItMatters: Liquidity explains why a profitable business can still run short of cash.

terms.definition: Pairs every row of one table with every row of another under no condition at all, so the output is m × n rows — 50 products against 12 months yields 600. A two-table query whose join condition is left off collapses into one, which is how a query over 1,000 and 2,000 rows returns 2,000,000 and freezes the report.
terms.whyItMatters: A troubleshooting item shows a report that suddenly returns millions of rows from two small tables; the multiplication, not the data, explains it.

terms.definition: Reinterpreting a situation until the required feeling is genuinely experienced, so expression and emotion match — as against surface acting, where a smile is layered over an unchanged feeling. The two produce the same visible behavior with opposite costs, because it is the mismatch inside surface acting, not the effort of acting, that drives exhaustion.
terms.whyItMatters: Coaching roleplays where a supervisor must help a frustrated employee face the public are graded on teaching the employee to reframe the customer's motive rather than just ordering a better face.

terms.definition: Employment term routing disputes to a private arbitrator instead of a court, waiving a jury and usually class treatment; the Federal Arbitration Act makes it binding and the award is nearly unappealable on the merits. The 2022 Ending Forced Arbitration Act carves out sexual assault and harassment claims, which an employee may still take to court.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay walking a new hire through an offer packet has to flag what this clause gives up, since signing happens on day one and matters years later.

terms.definition: Boundaries drawn three standard deviations above and below the process mean and calculated FROM the process's own output, which makes them a statement of what the process does — specification limits are set by the customer or engineer and state what the product must be, so a process can sit inside one pair and outside the other.
terms.whyItMatters: The classic exam trap shows points inside the charted band but outside customer tolerance; recognizing that a stable process can still be producing unacceptable parts is the tested discrimination.

terms.definition: A mindset committed to meeting customer needs and providing quality help.
terms.whyItMatters: It helps employees deliver consistent, customer-focused interactions.

terms.definition: Albert Mehrabian's finding that when a speaker's words, tone and facial expression contradict each other about how they feel, listeners resolve the conflict by weighting words 7 percent, tone of voice 38 percent, and facial expression 55 percent. The routine misuse is the claim that 93 percent of all communication is nonverbal: the studies tested single words about liking, said by women, in a laboratory, and say nothing about the content of an informational message. Cited correctly, it covers incongruence only.
terms.whyItMatters: It is the standard trap answer on nonverbal-communication items, and a judge who has heard the '93 percent' line all day notices the competitor who states its actual scope.

terms.definition: Fraction of checkable deposits a bank is barred from lending — mandated reserves ÷ deposits. At 10%, a $1,000 deposit locks up $100 and frees $900, and the ceiling on deposit creation is 1 ÷ 0.10 = 10; cutting the ratio to 5% doubles that ceiling without the central bank buying a single security.
terms.whyItMatters: Interest-rate-fluctuation items ask how a change in this one fraction moves the amount of money in circulation, and the answer is the reciprocal.

terms.definition: The percentage of candidates who move from one recruiting stage to the next — 400 applicants producing 80 screens is a 20% yield, and 80 screens producing 20 interviews is 25%. Chained backward, the stage yields tell a recruiter how many applicants the top of the funnel must hold to end with a set number of hires: 5 hires at these rates requires roughly 400 applicants.
terms.whyItMatters: Hiring-plan roleplays ask how many applications a posting must attract for four openings, which is solved by multiplying the stage yields, not by guessing.

terms.definition: Matching a checkbook or ledger against a bank statement by adjusting both sides — outstanding checks and deposits in transit on the bank's, fees and interest on the depositor's.
terms.whyItMatters: A finance exam item gives a statement balance and a book balance and asks for the true cash figure; only adjusting one side gets it wrong.

terms.definition: The 128-bit addressing scheme succeeding the 32-bit scheme the internet was built on. Because each added bit doubles the space, 128 bits is not four times larger but 2^96 times larger — the older scheme's roughly 4.3 billion addresses ran out, and the newer one is written as eight hexadecimal groups rather than four decimal ones.
terms.whyItMatters: An item on the scope of the internet asks why address exhaustion forced a change instead of an expansion; the doubling, not the label, is the explanation.

terms.definition: Four-quadrant triage that sorts a task list on two separate axes, urgency and importance: important and urgent is handled now, important and not urgent is scheduled and is where career-building work lives, urgent and not important is delegated, and neither is dropped. The insight is that a loud task can rank last.
terms.whyItMatters: A management roleplay handed a full inbox and one afternoon is scored on the quadrant each item lands in and the action that quadrant dictates.

terms.definition: Amplification of demand variability moving upstream, where a small retail sales swing becomes a larger distributor order swing and a still larger factory order swing, driven by batch ordering, price promotions, forecast updating and shortage gaming — shared point-of-sale data damps it.
terms.whyItMatters: Supply-chain collaboration roleplays use this to justify sharing real sales data with suppliers, and the four named causes are what turn a vague answer about 'communication' into a scored one.

terms.definition: The share of contacts answered inside a stated number of seconds, written as a pair — the industry default target is 80% answered within 20 seconds, and the other 20% may wait any length of time at all. That blind spot is why it is reported alongside average speed of answer rather than instead of it.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay that asks a competitor to set a staffing target for a holiday peak wants this pair of numbers, not a promise to answer quickly.

terms.definition: The benefit a customer believes they receive compared with the cost or effort.
terms.whyItMatters: Value helps explain why a customer chooses one offer over another.

terms.definition: Presenting numbers and trends visually so patterns are clear.
terms.whyItMatters: Visuals make recommendations look credible and actionable.

terms.definition: Sum of the market shares of the four biggest sellers: 18 + 15 + 9 + 6 = 48%. Crossing roughly 40% marks an industry as an oligopoly, and 100% is a monopoly or a tight cartel — but because it adds shares without squaring them, it cannot tell four equal firms apart from one giant and three minnows.
terms.whyItMatters: Competition questions give a share table and ask for the structure label plus its threshold, and the blind spot is exactly what the follow-up tests.

terms.definition: Paying a loan off through fixed installments split between interest and principal, with the interest share largest at the start and shrinking every payment.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items ask why an early mortgage payment barely reduces the balance; the amortization split is the reason, not a fee.

terms.definition: A 32-bit pattern splitting an address into a network part and a host part: a /24 leaves 8 bits for hosts, which is 2^8 = 256 addresses, of which 254 are assignable once the network and broadcast addresses come out. A /25 halves that to 126 usable, so borrowing a single bit costs half the room on the segment.
terms.whyItMatters: Asked how many devices a store's network segment can hold, the competitor must convert the slash number into host bits and then subtract 2 — the raw power of two is the wrong answer.

terms.definition: Sworn statement the CEO and CFO sign with every quarterly and annual report, affirming that it is accurate and that they evaluated the effectiveness of disclosure controls as of the period's end. Section 906 supplies the teeth: a knowing false certification carries fines up to $5 million and imprisonment up to 20 years.
terms.whyItMatters: An accounting roleplay about pressure to delay recognizing an expense is answered by naming who personally signs for the numbers and what the penalty is.

terms.definition: Adams's model in which an employee compares their own outcome-to-input ratio against a referent other's ratio and, when the two ratios differ, restores balance by cutting effort, demanding more reward, or changing the comparison target; perceived fairness, not absolute pay, drives the response.
terms.whyItMatters: Roleplays about a well-paid employee who resents a colleague's raise are scored on the ratio comparison and on which restoration behavior to expect.

terms.definition: The width of the customer's tolerance divided by six standard deviations of process spread, with Cpk penalizing an off-center mean by measuring only the nearer specification limit; 1.33 is the common minimum and a value below 1.0 means defects are unavoidable even when the process is perfectly stable.
terms.whyItMatters: Supplier-quality roleplays use this figure as the acceptance bar: a supplier can hold a steady process and still fail, which is the argument you make when resolving a quality dispute.

terms.definition: Contacts that disconnect while waiting divided by contacts offered — 90 hang-ups out of 3,000 offered is 3%, and most centers exclude calls dropped inside the first 5 seconds as misdials before reporting it. Under 5% is the common acceptance band, and the number rises non-linearly once average wait passes the caller's patience threshold.
terms.whyItMatters: Exam items hand over the offered and abandoned counts and expect both the percentage and the staffing conclusion drawn from it.

terms.definition: The nonverbal channel of body motion - posture, gesture, facial expression and eye behavior - which is distinct from paralanguage, the vocal qualities wrapped around the words (pitch, rate, volume, pauses, filled hesitations like 'um'), and from chronemics, the messages carried by the use of time such as arriving late, answering after three days, or scheduling only 10 minutes. Naming the right channel matters because each has a different repair.
terms.whyItMatters: Items that ask you to read a supervisor's crossed arms, clipped tone and delayed reply are testing three separate channels in one scenario.

terms.definition: (Price − marginal cost) ÷ price, running from 0 under perfect competition to near 1 for an unchallenged monopolist. A $50 price on $40 of marginal cost scores 0.20, and because the figure equals the reciprocal of demand elasticity, a firm facing elasticity of 5 can hold only a 20% markup over marginal cost.
terms.whyItMatters: Pricing-power items ask how much a firm can charge above its own marginal cost, and the elasticity link converts a demand estimate into a markup ceiling.

terms.definition: Current assets divided by current liabilities, the standard test of whether a business can cover what it owes within the next twelve months.
terms.whyItMatters: Finance exam items hand over a balance sheet and ask whether the firm can meet short-term obligations; a ratio under 1.0 is the answer that says no.

terms.definition: A machine-readable tagging standard the SEC requires in filings, attaching a defined element to every reported figure so that one firm's net revenue line and another's total revenues line resolve to the same concept and load into an analyst's model without anyone rekeying them.
terms.whyItMatters: Technology questions ask how thousands of filings get screened automatically, and standardized tagging rather than a spreadsheet import is the answer.

terms.definition: Hits divided by total lookups — 900 of 1,000 is 90%. Read as percentage points the figure misleads: moving from 90% to 95% cuts the 100 misses that reach the database down to 50, so a five-point gain halves backend load, and the last few points are worth far more than the first.
terms.whyItMatters: A technology-impact item asks whether a small improvement to a caching layer is worth the spend; the answer runs on misses removed, not on the headline percentage.

terms.definition: Allocation of professional growth into three ratios: 70% from challenging on-the-job assignments, 20% from developmental relationships such as coaching and feedback, and only 10% from formal courses. It reframes a development plan away from a training catalog and toward the stretch assignment that produces most of the learning.
terms.whyItMatters: A roleplay building a development plan for a high-potential employee loses points if the whole plan is a list of seminars.

terms.definition: Unit price plus freight, insurance, duties and tariffs, customs brokerage, and handling to the receiving dock — the total that makes an offshore quote comparable to a domestic one, which is why the lower quoted unit price frequently loses once every downstream charge is added.
terms.whyItMatters: Vendor-selection roleplays present a cheaper overseas bid and expect you to reject a comparison based on quoted price alone by adding the delivery-related charges before deciding.

terms.definition: The commitment a company makes about the value and experience it will deliver.
terms.whyItMatters: Knowing the promise helps employees deliver a consistent experience.

terms.definition: The parliamentary manual whose thresholds get tested: a main motion needs a second and passes on a simple majority of votes cast, an amendment needs a majority, closing debate by moving the previous question needs two-thirds because it takes away a member's right to speak, and a tie fails. Precedence governs order - while an amendment is pending, no new main motion is in order - and a point of order can interrupt because it concerns the rules rather than the question.
terms.whyItMatters: Officer and staff-meeting scenarios ask what vote a motion requires, and the two-thirds threshold for cutting off debate is the one competitors miss.

terms.definition: Protection granted to original works of authorship such as writing, music, and art.
terms.whyItMatters: Digital content and creative works are critical assets in modern business.
